story.headline: Ethiopian army enters Tigray capital Mekelle
story.summary: Ethiopian federal troops entered Mekelle on Saturday 3 October as the rebel TPLF withdrew from the Tigray capital and signalled a shift to guerrilla war.
story.display_body: Ethiopian federal troops entered Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, on Saturday 3 October, after the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF — the party that ran Tigray and dominated Ethiopia's government for nearly three decades until 2018) withdrew its forces from the city. A humanitarian source told AFP that federal units and their allies were seen "at several points" in Mekelle with no immediate fighting reported; a local journalist said TPLF leaders and troops were leaving, weapons in hand, as the army advanced. The offensive, which reopened in late September, pits the federal army and allied Fano militias from neighbouring Amhara against the TPLF, which in April expelled the federally-appointed Tigray administration and again openly defied Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. TPLF president Debretsion Gebremichael, in a video on Thursday, appeared to accept the setback and signalled a switch to guerrilla warfare: "Our strategy is to strike the enemy where we want." The sequence echoes 2020–2022, when the federal army took Mekelle in three weeks, lost it to a TPLF counter-offensive in 2021, and finally agreed a truce in late 2022 — a deal whose key terms were never implemented. Telecommunications across Tigray are heavily disrupted, making independent verification difficult, and neither the army nor Abiy's office answered AFP's queries.
story.why: the recapture of the regional capital marks a sharp escalation of a war the 2022 Pretoria agreement was meant to end, and observers warn it could draw in Eritrea and Sudan — a diplomatic source said the presidents of Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia and Sudan's army chief would meet in Alamein, Egypt, on Sunday 4 October on the sidelines of an African business forum.

story.headline: Houthis claim Aramco strike as Yemen war surges
story.summary: Yemen's Houthis said they hit an Aramco site in Riyadh; the Saudi-led coalition called the claim misleading as fighting sharply intensified.
story.display_body: Yemen's Houthis said on Saturday 3 October they had struck a Saudi Aramco facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, as fighting between the Iran-aligned movement and Yemen's Saudi-backed government sharply intensified. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, in a statement on X, called the operation "precise and direct"; a plume of smoke and fire was photographed near an Aramco site south of Riyadh the same day. The Saudi-led coalition's spokesman, Turki al-Maliki, dismissed the strike claim as "misleading" — the two accounts have not been independently reconciled. Early on Sunday 4 October the coalition said it had carried out 97 "precise targeting operations" against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha and Taiz fronts; a Yemeni government spokesman put the toll at "at least 260" Houthi fighters, a figure that cannot be verified. The fighting has escalated since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July 2026; in mid-September the Houthis seized the port of Mocha and islands commanding the Bab al-Mandeb strait — a chokepoint for global oil shipping — before anti-Houthi forces steadied the lines.
story.why: attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and casualty claims from both sides point to the widest Yemen flare-up since the truce broke down, with hundreds of thousands already displaced and the Red Sea shipping lane again exposed.

story.headline: Latvia's pro-EU United List wins election
story.summary: PM Andris Kulbergs' pro-European United List won Latvia's legislative election with a record 35.3 percent and 42 of 100 Saeima seats.
story.display_body: Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' pro-European United List won Latvia's legislative election held on Saturday 3 October, taking a record 35.3% of the vote and 42 of the Saeima's 100 seats, near-final results from the Baltic state's electoral commission showed on Sunday 4 October. It is the strongest result for any party since Latvia regained independence in 1990, though turnout was low at 51.8%. Kulbergs, a former private-sector executive new to politics, called it a vote for "change" in a country of 1.8 million grappling with economic stagnation and demographic decline; he must now assemble a majority coalition. Two of his current centre-right partners — the nationalist National Alliance (8.9%, 10 seats) and the centrist New Unity (6.3%, 7 seats) — cleared the 5% threshold, but a third, the Union of Greens and Farmers, fell short; without it the bloc holds 50.5% of the vote. Security dominated the campaign in the EU and NATO member, which borders Russia and Belarus and spends close to 5% of GDP on defence; most parties likely to enter parliament back more military spending and continued aid to Ukraine.
story.why: the result keeps a frontline Baltic state firmly on its pro-EU, pro-Ukraine course, even as populist challengers gained ground.

story.headline: Federal fix unblocks stalled Zurich housing
story.summary: A federal round table agreed to narrow how the ISOS heritage inventory is applied, unblocking some 4,000 stalled flats in Zurich.
story.display_body: A federal round table has agreed to narrow how the heritage-protection inventory ISOS (the Federal Inventory of Sites Worthy of Protection) is applied, a change authorities say will unblock housing projects stalled by conservation disputes — notably some 4,000 flats in the city of Zurich, SRF reported on Saturday 3 October. The inventory covers around 1,200 sites, from Zurich and Basel to small villages; because obligations can be derived from a listing, projects were delayed or blocked — three-quarters of Zurich's area falls under ISOS. The flagship case is the ASIG cooperative's Dreispitz estate in Zurich-Schwamendingen, where plans for roughly 1,000 flats were held up as long as two years. After the city appealed to the Confederation in 2024 over planning and legal uncertainty, the Federal Office of Culture convened the parties and brokered a solution: ISOS will in future be applied directly only where a project genuinely affects the character of a townscape.
story.why: housing shortage and construction costs are among the sharpest everyday pressures in Swiss cities, and narrowing a federal conservation rule that had frozen thousands of flats is a concrete lever on supply — though it trades some heritage protection for building capacity.

story.headline: Swiss Steel to cut more German jobs
story.summary: Swiss Steel announced a further restructuring focused on its German sites that will bring additional job cuts, its CEO said.
story.display_body: Swiss Steel, the Lucerne-headquartered steelmaker, has announced a further restructuring that will fall on its German sites and bring more job cuts, chief executive Frank Koch said in an interview with the SonntagsZeitung published on Sunday 4 October. Koch gave no figures for the planned cuts but said the move would "significantly" reduce the group's dependence on the automotive business and reposition its plants for a much-shrunken market. The company, long loss-making, has run through repeated rounds of cost-cutting.
story.why: Swiss Steel is one of the country's last large industrial manufacturers, and renewed cuts underline how Europe's steel sector is still contracting under weak demand and high energy costs.
